description: VITALASTRO is a NASA Space Apps Challenge project that improves astronaut healthcare on missions to the Moon or Mars, where communication delays with Earth can reach 40 minutes. The app monitors vital signs in real time, detects anomalies and triggers alerts without relying on the Internet, while offering guided emergency procedures. In a second phase, AI will analyze each astronaut’s medical history to anticipate health problems. It enables fast, autonomous care even when Earth is too far away.
summary:
- In 2019, an astronaut aboard the ISS suffered a potentially fatal jugular deep vein thrombosis. Because Low Earth Orbit allows near-instant communication, Houston Flight Surgeons diagnosed the clot remotely and ordered immediate anticoagulant injections. However, in upcoming lunar and Martian missions, round-trip communication delays reach up to 44 minutes—making Earth-dependent emergency medicine impossible.
- Our solution provides *real-time, offline medical autonomy* without adding a single gram of new flight hardware. Instead of waiting for satellite downlinks to Houston, our edge software intercepts vital telemetry directly at the spacecraft’s onboard server hub from NASA’s existing biomedical sensors (ultrasound, ECG, pulse oximetry, dosimeters, and thermal loops).
- A lightweight, offline-first *Smartwatch & Crew App* displays these markers on a high-contrast biometric dashboard. When critical thresholds breach—indicating thrombosis, acute hypoxia, malignant arrhythmia, solar radiation spikes, or suit heatstroke—the watch triggers an instant local alarm and guides crewmates through step-by-step, life-saving action protocols. When Earth cannot answer in time, our software saves lives.
details:
Real-Time Medical Autonomy for Deep Space

Research, Clinical Architecture, and Smartwatch Alert System for Lunar and Martian Missions

1. Executive Summary & Core Vision

The transition from Low Earth Orbit (LEO) exploration to deep space travel presents a fundamental operational challenge: the loss of real-time communication with Earth-based medical teams. This project establishes an architecture for real-time, fully offline medical autonomy tailored for crewed missions to the Moon and Mars. For vital cases that need a fast reaction.

Core Architectural Philosophy

We do not propose or develop new physical hardware or sensors. Introducing novel flight hardware adds mass, power requirements, and multi-year launch certification cycles. Instead, our software architecture integrates directly into NASA's existing biomedical hardware and telemetry infrastructure. The system operates by intercepting vital biomarker telemetry locally at the spacecraft's onboard server hub prior to long-distance satellite transmission and Earth downlink.

End-User Solution

The user-facing system consists of a lightweight, offline-first Smartwatch & Crew App (ESA is already using a modified Samsung Galaxy). This platform:

  • Ingests multi-parameter biomedical feeds locally in real time.
  • Displays astronaut vital status across an intuitive biometric dashboard designed for high-stress operational environments.
  • Triggers instantaneous, local haptic, visual, and auditory alarms when physiological markers breach predefined safety thresholds.
  • Renders clear, step-by-step emergency action plans to guide crew members through immediate clinical interventions without requiring ground control input.

2. The Problem: The Communication Latency Wall & Historical Precedents

Historical Precedents in Spaceflight Medicine

International Space Station (2019 DVT Incident)

During a routine vascular research study (Fluid Shifts) approximately 50 days into an ISS mission, an ultrasound scan revealed an asymptomatic Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) in an astronaut's left internal jugular vein.

Because the ISS operates in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), communication latency between the station and the Mission Control Center (MCC) in Houston is minimal (less than two seconds). Flight Surgeons rapidly consulted external experts, including Dr. Stephan Moll, to establish a remote treatment plan. The crew administered onboard enoxaparin injections followed by oral apixaban delivered via a subsequent resupply vehicle, preventing a potentially fatal pulmonary embolism.

Additional Spaceflight Medical Incidents

  • Apollo 15 & Skylab: Crew members experienced cardiac arrhythmias (such as premature ventricular contractions and bigeminy), linked to potassium depletion, high workload, and cardiac stress under microgravity.
  • Salyut 7 (1985): A severe, acute infectious illness (prostatitis leading to sepsis risk) required the premature evacuation of Commander Vladimir Vasyutin back to Earth.
  • Mir (1997 Collision): A collision with a Progress supply vessel compromised cabin integrity, requiring immediate autonomous action by the crew to seal off the damaged Spektr module and deploy emergency oxygen support without waiting for ground intervention.
The Deep Space Bottleneck

For upcoming Artemis missions to the Lunar South Pole and future long-duration missions to Mars, the proximity advantage of LEO vanishes.

  • Lunar Missions: One-way communication delays average ~1.3 seconds, with local line-of-sight blackouts behind the Moon.
  • Martian Missions: Round-trip signal times range between 8 to 44 minutes, compounded by multi-day solar conjunction blackouts.

In acute, life-threatening medical conditions—such as severe hypoxia, malignant arrhythmias, or rapidly progressing heatstroke—waiting nearly an hour for ground telemetry analysis and clinical response is unacceptable. Astronauts must transition from a ground-dependent medical model to complete onboard, real-time decision support.

3. Existing NASA Biomedical Hardware & Telemetry Infrastructure

Our platform leverages the extensive health monitoring ecosystem currently fielded or qualified by NASA and partner agencies:

Hardware & Wearables
  • Continuous Biometric Wearables: Hexoskin-style smart shirts and chest straps providing multi-lead continuous Electrocardiography (ECG), Heart Rate Variability (HRV), and respiratory inductance plethysmography.
  • Smartwatches & Actigraphy: Modified wearable devices monitoring activity levels, surface temperature, and Photoplethysmography (PPG).
  • Portable Ultrasound Devices: Compact ultrasound units (such as Butterfly iQ or similar flight-qualified systems) used for Vascular checks, Ocular Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) protocols, and Cardiac evaluations.
  • Diagnostic & Environmental Sensors: Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGM), point-of-care blood/saliva/urine analyzers, ingestible core temperature pills, Liquid Cooling and Ventilation Garment (LCVG) thermal sensors, and active personal radiation dosimeters (TEPC/OSLD) alongside spacecraft Radiation Environment Monitors (REM).
Software & Ground Infrastructure

Under standard operational workflows, raw sensor feeds aggregate at the onboard crew server / telemetry hub. The server packages these data streams for uplink to satellite relays (e.g., TDRS, Deep Space Network) and downlinks them to the Mission Control Center (MCC) at Johnson Space Center (JSC). Ground teams process these metrics using systems like MIST (Medical Information Systems and Tools) and long-term Electronic Health Record (EHR) platforms. Autonomous offline initiatives, such as HERMES and the EXPAND database (TRISH), represent early shifts toward local data architecture.

4. The 5 Critical Acute Pathologies, Sensor Markers & Action Plans

We identified five acute medical conditions that represent immediate threats to life or mission integrity. These conditions require immediate local detection and execution of clinical protocols within seconds to minutes, making them unsuited for Earth-dependent workflows.

Critical Pathology

Existing NASA Sensor Source

Key Biomarkers & Trigger Thresholds

Immediate Autonomous Action Plan

Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

Portable Onboard Ultrasound & Bioelectrical Impedance / Plethysmography

Decreased flow velocity or stasis in internal jugular/femoral veins; abnormal vessel echogenicity; local fluid shift anomalies.

Administer emergency subcutaneous anticoagulant (enoxaparin/heparin autoinjector) via guided on-screen dosage protocol.

Acute Hypoxia & Hypercapnia

Optical Pulse Oximeters (Wearable/Suit PPG) & NDIR Infrared Helmet/Cabin Gas Analyzers

SpO2 dropping below 90% (or rapid >5% decline); inspired CO2 partial pressure ($PiCO2$) exceeding safety limits.

Trigger emergency suit O2 purge, don portable oxygen mask, abort EVA, or isolate affected habitat module.

Malignant Cardiac Arrhythmias

Continuous 1-to-3 Lead ECG Biometric Shirts & Chest Straps

Resting HR >160 bpm or <40 bpm (symptomatic); chaotic HRV; wide QRS complexes; prolonged QT; absence of P-waves.

Administer antiarrhythmic medication if conscious; if unresponding/VFib, initiate CPR and deploy AED guided by app.

Acute Radiation Exposure (SPE)

Active Personal Dosimeters (TEPC/OSLD) & Spacecraft REM

Absorbed dose rate spiking above 50–100 mSv/h; rapid high-energy proton flux surge from Coronal Mass Ejection.

Abort external tasks immediately; evacuate crew to the onboard shielded Storm Shelter (water-shielded core).

Heatstroke / Suit Hyperthermia

Ingestible Core Temp Pill, Skin Thermal Sensors, LCVG Loop Sensors

Core body temp rising rapidly above 38.5°C–39.0°C; return-water temp anomaly in suit cooling loop.

Halt physical exertion immediately; switch suit backup cooling valve to maximum flow; return to airlock.

5. Solution Architecture: Onboard Interception & Smartwatch App

The system integrates directly into existing mission operations without introducing hardware mass or altering primary flight instrumentation:

[ NASA Biomedical Sensors / Wearables ]

                  │

                  ▼

   [ Onboard Telemetry Server / Hub ]

                  │

                  ├──────────────────────────────┐

                  ▼                              ▼

    [ Earth Downlink (DSN / TDRS) ]   [ OUR EDGE SERVICE ]

      (Subject to 40m Latency)                   │ (Local Interception)

                                                 ▼

                                     [ Smartwatch & Crew App ]

                                                 │

                                                 ▼

                                     [ Real-Time Alarm & Plan ]

Step 1: Pre-Downlink Onboard Server Interception

Instead of waiting for telemetry to pass through the Deep Space Network pipeline, an lightweight edge service runs locally on the spacecraft's primary server. This service taps directly into the local telemetry stream where sensor data is continuously aggregated.

Here of the specific markers and telemetry parameters to extract from existing NASA sensors to detect each of the 5 critical risks:

  1. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

    • Existing Sensors: Portable Onboard Ultrasound & Bioelectrical Impedance / Plethysmography.
  • Markers to Extract:

    • Decreased blood flow velocity or venous stasis in the internal jugular or femoral veins.
  • Abnormal vessel echogenicity indicating thrombus (clot) formation.
  • Localized fluid shift anomalies.
  1. Acute Hypoxia & Hypercapnia (Low O2 / High CO2)

    • Existing Sensors: Optical Pulse Oximeters (Wearable/Suit PPG) & NDIR Infrared Helmet/Cabin Gas Analyzers.
  • Markers to Extract:

    • Peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) dropping below 90% (or a rapid decline of >5%).
  • Inspired carbon dioxide partial pressure (PiCO2) exceeding safety thresholds in the helmet or cabin.
  1. Malignant Cardiac Arrhythmias (Ventricular Tachycardia / Fibrillation)

    • Existing Sensors: Continuous 1-to-3 Lead ECG Biometric Shirts & Chest Straps.
  • Markers to Extract:
  • Resting heart rate extremes (>160 bpm or <40 bpm with symptoms).
  • Chaotic Heart Rate Variability (HRV).
  • Morphological ECG abnormalities (wide QRS complexes, prolonged QT intervals, or absence of P-waves).
  1. Acute Radiation Exposure (Solar Particle Event - SPE)

    • Existing Sensors: Active Personal Dosimeters (TEPC/OSLD) & Spacecraft Radiation Environment Monitors (REM).
  • Markers to Extract:

    • Absorbed dose rate spiking above safety limits (50–100 mSv/h).
  • Exponential surges in high-energy proton flux resulting from Coronal Mass Ejections.
  1. Heatstroke / Suit Hyperthermia

    • Existing Sensors: Ingestible Core Temperature Pills, Skin Thermal Sensors, & Liquid Cooling and Ventilation Garment (LCVG) Loop Sensors.
  • Markers to Extract:
  • Core body temperature rising rapidly above 38.5°C – 39.0°C.
  • Abnormal return-water temperature increases within the suit's cooling loop.
Step 2: Real-Time Smartwatch & Crew App

The application layer runs locally on crew smartwatches and tablet interfaces (spacewalk suit). Built offline-first, it operates independently of external network availability or ground control links.

Step 3: Biometric Dashboard

The interface presents a high-contrast dashboard displaying five critical physiological vectors:

  1. Vascular / Hemodynamic: Flow status and clot risk.
  2. Respiratory / Gas Exchange: Real-time SpO2 and ambient/helmet $CO2$.
  3. Cardiovascular: Live ECG trace analysis and arrhythmia classification.
  4. Radiological Environment: Cumulative dose and real-time mSv/h rate.
  5. Thermoregulatory: Core body temperature and cooling loop delta.
Step 4: Instant Local Alarm & Actionable Protocol Engine

When telemetry crosses a defined risk threshold, the app triggers immediate haptic, visual, and audible alerts on the crew member's wearable device. The application automatically bypasses high-level summaries to present an emergency checklist, offering step-by-step guidance for crew-assisted intervention.

Here is the direct list of immediate actions in English for each of the 5 critical conditions:

  1. Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT)

    • Immediate Action: Administer an emergency subcutaneous anticoagulant (enoxaparin/heparin autoinjector) following the guided on-screen dosage protocol.
    • Immediate Action: Trigger the emergency oxygen purge in the spacesuit, don a portable oxygen mask, abort the EVA, or immediately isolate the affected habitat module.
  2. Malignant Cardiac Arrhythmias (Ventricular Tachycardia / Fibrillation)
  • Immediate Action: Administer antiarrhythmic rescue medication if conscious; if unresponsive or in ventricular fibrillation, initiate immediate CPR and deploy the onboard Automated External Defibrillator (AED) guided step-by-step by the app.
  1. Acute Radiation Exposure (Solar Particle Event - SPE)

    • Immediate Action: Immediately abort all external tasks and evacuate the crew to the spacecraft's shielded Storm Shelter (water-shielded core) until the particle flux subsides.
    • Immediate Action: Halt all physical exertion immediately to stop metabolic heat generation, switch the suit's backup cooling valve (LCVG) to maximum flow, and return to the airlock.

6. Phase 2 Roadmap: Edge GPU & Personalized AI (RHAI Systems)

Following the initial MVP deployment, further scalability focuses on integrating local AI inference capabilities, giving the solution a full stack of data and predictive capabilities. We can use the development that is in research right now between ESA and the spanish company RHAI Systems:

  • Onboard Edge GPU Infrastructure: Deploy optimized local machine learning models using RHAI Systems  AI (RHAI) platforms engineered for radiation-hardened edge computing hardware.
  • Personalized Baseline Adaptation: Integrate each astronaut's historical Electronic Health Record (EHR) data into the edge model. By evaluating real-time telemetry against an individual's specific baseline rather than population averages, the system can detect subtle physiological drift—predicting acute events like early-stage venous stasis or pre-arrhythmic conditions prior to critical threshold breaches.
